en: Ruiners of the people, utterly vile,
Let there be no ignorant fools!”
Chewing white-wheat bread,
The champions in the open steppe
Clasped the holy Quran;
Taking knives from their sheaths,
They cut a twig:
“Let this be our pledge!” they said,
Dipping their hands in blood.
Speaking in the open steppe,
Have you seen lion Manas!
The finest, lion Manas,
Khan Bakay, Bay's son,
Azhybay, Argyn Khan's son—
Newly come into view,
The leader of the forty companions,
Golden words ringing from his mouth,
Your noble Bakay began to speak,
Speaking softly, laying words down firmly.
One word of his was a thousand gold coins;
He was Bakay, the learned lion.
Addressing Azhybay,
Your generous elder Bakay's
Words were these:
“Last summer,
My child Azhybay, listen:
Looking for wild asses, chasing antelope,
I went on a long hunting expedition.
Fit for a blood-drinking hero,
The living gun Akkelte,
Within the pine woods,
I left hidden in a cache.
Before I came back again,
They utterly ruined me;
They stole that gun away.
I hear it is a city with a princely court.
Akkelte, the dear khan's gun,
Let us somehow ask for it and take it.
If they give the short gun back,
Let us give our thanks,
Let us return without quarrelling.
If they will not heed our words,
If they will not give Akkelte,
Let us go coaxing and cajoling.
If they give the short gun back,
Let us part without ill feeling!”
Manas and Azhybay said:
“Heroic elder, agreed.
The one who will not simply give it to you—
All seven of his forefathers are infidels!”
Leading the way, they set out,
Sparing no horses, traveling far,
To a spur of broken steppe,
To a pine-covered headland,
They arrived and stood.
Your accomplished Bakay, the leopard,
Spoke well-considered words:
“My fellow sleeper, sharing my lodging,
Whose fame is heard among the people,
Ah, Azhybay, my interpreter!
An elder with the bearing of a saint,
I am Bakay the destroyer.
The finest at leveling a spear,
I am thirty-five years old,
Older than the rest of you.
Choose Kartküröng, take the horse;
From blood-drinking Manas and Bakay,
Take a letter the size of a palm.
To the settlement of the courtly people,
Go ask for Akkelte and return!
For God's sake, for our sake,
If death comes, go and die!
Go speak sweet words;
It was a keen weapon granted by fortune;
Bring Akkelte back!
The many doors and gates,
Carefully learn them all.
Say, ‘Give us Akkelte,’
Pour out abundant words.
Its openings and gaps,
Observe and learn them thoroughly!
Tell us how many soldiers are in their army;
If they do not give Akkelte,
Come at once and tell their answer!
Go in health and return unharmed.
An envoy is not put to death;
Come quickly, before we long for you.
Knowing seventy different tongues,
My accomplished one, we chose you;
Do not shrink from this task.
The dark ridge we rely upon—
‘He is our support,’ we said, and sent you.
Never sated with drinking blood,
‘He is a lion,’ we said, and sent you.
We listened to your words with honor.
Khan Azhybay, my twin,
We have chosen you.
Akkelte is precious;
Ask insistently and bring it back.
If they will not heed your words,
If they will not give Akkelte,
The decree that Allah wrote,
If he lays it on your head, face it there.
If they happen to humiliate you,
Do not remain alive—die there!
There will be pines and dense woodland;
Push along the single path.
‘At last I have met my death,’ say,
And go, giving up hope of life.
The appointed time is two days;
If you are gone beyond two days,
‘Azhybay has died,’ we shall say,
And charge straight in, thrusting spears;
We shall set the trouble straight.
Thundering in combat,
We shall return through mutual slaughter.
Azhybay, after you,
Lion Bakay and Khan Manas,
We shall follow into death!
Shouting and thrusting spears,
Coming out to fight in single combat,
Standing face to face,
Firing guns, drawing bows,
Striking with wet thuds in battle,
Against the hairy-mouthed people
We shall wage a savage war.
My Azhybay, for your sake,
We shall perish to the last!
Its name was left in the cache;
This work is no easy thing,
This trouble over Akkelte.
If we do not get Akkelte,
If we do not stand proud and bold,
Let us sink away unborn,
For the sake of Akkelte,
Let us die grappling in combat.
They seem to be a maddened people;
Let us show our proud strength!
Their manner is strange, their wrath fierce;
From the place where I cached it,
They stole it this autumn.
If they do not give Akkelte,
Say, ‘We are dead,’ and abandon hope of life!
The living gun Akkelte—
How can we rest without getting it?
Because of what has happened,
For the sake of Akkelte,
A merciless slaughter—
How can we rest without bringing it?
Such is the nature of Akkelte:
It was a keen weapon of joined steel;
Leveled at a maddened enemy,
It was a treasure that would shatter them.
An apple-headed gun of outstanding steel,
Disregarding distance, far or near,
Not failing for sixty days,
It was a keen weapon to carry,
A treasure that could not be found.
This possession of mine is precious;
To tell you about Akkelte,
It is worth a world's livestock.
My champion, my Azhy, listen!
We have driven our lives after it;
Let us face slaughter now,
For the pain of losing Akkelte.
Its matchcord silk, its strap gold,
Even if we labored a thousand years,
Nothing like Akkelte would come our way.
The youngest of the six lions,
Allah's beloved mortal,
Generous Lord Manas—
Nothing like it was ever found for him.
It was a treasure to carry,
For blue-maned lion Manas
It was a fitting keen weapon.
When I think of Akkelte,
I burn within, my liver is embers.
Azhybay, going as mediator,
If you show your lion's nature,
If you put Akkelte into our hands,
Your elder, old Bakay,
Would have no regret if he died now!
If they should happen to give it,
If they should chance to hand it over!
Let me describe Akkelte:
Let them not beguile you
And give you another gun!
‘A gun for your gun,’ they might say,
Deceiving you by chance—
Let them not put their feet up against the wall,
Let them not play their trumpet tune.
The identifying mark of Akkelte:
Along one edge of its strap
There is clearly inscribed writing.
If you read and examine the writing,
There is leopard Manas's name.
If you consider Akkelte,
It is a treasure worth Beijing.
To Beijing of Kakan-Chin,
To the swarming Chinese,
It is the keen weapon that brings havoc.
If you fail to get it, disgrace;
Such is each identifying mark.
My precious Azhy, my blue-maned one,
Akkelte is entrusted to you!
You know the measure of words;
You will go on disputing.
There is much to say if one tells it.
Your heroism upon your brow,
Gather it there, my brave Azhy, and go.
Speaking words of goodwill,
Go ask for Akkelte.
Enter their palace and return;
The supremely precious Akkelte,
Learn where it is and return.
Without quarrelling or bickering,
Tell them to hear our words.
If they do not give Akkelte,
Tell them to come out where guns will fire.
The envoy who has come by choice,
Tell them to hear his honored words.
If they do not hear honored words,
Tell them to come out to the field of combat!
If they provoke us, will God let them be?
Will one who fears death prosper?
Speak firmly, without wavering:
Say, ‘Give us Akkelte.’
‘If you do not give Akkelte,
To the place where you will fight with guns,
Come out now!’—say that!
If you take fright, disgrace;
You are a champion, Azhybay;
Take someone with you as your death-pillow!”
While Bakay was saying this,
The blue-maned lion of surpassing fortune,
Generous Manas, the leopard,
Holding his hands behind his back,
The formidable hero who had stood motionless,
Huge as a towering mountain,
Toward the prancing dun horse
Strode in his great bulk.
From behind the horse Akkula,
From the rear of his saddle,
From the top of his saddle cushion,
Bound back and fastened close,
Secured to the saddle thongs,
He untied the blue saddlebags.
Their pattern embroidered in gold,
That formidable one's stout saddlebags—
When he took them, most impressive,
Wrapped about with silk,
Bound it about with silver.
Covered with fine fibers,
Overlaid with leather,
To find their owners and give them over,
Your dear lord had kept them safe.
